An 11-year-old female patient with a prior history of cardiac arrest arrived at the emergency room (ER) 35 minutes after losing consciousness. Her mother had immediately administered basic life support. The patient was born in the 40th gestational week by normal spontaneous vaginal delivery and weighed 4.0 kg. There was no specific family history of syncope or sudden cardiac death. Six years ago, she experienced a brief syncopal episode. Electroencephalography (EEG) at that time showed no specific abnormality. Six months after this first event, she was admitted to the ER for sudden loss of consciousness. Ventricular fibrillation (VF) was noted, and the normal sinus rhythm was restored by defibrillation. Neither delta wave nor QT interval prolongation was observed on a resting electrocardiogram (ECG) (). Echocardiography did not reveal any structural abnormalities, and Holter monitoring did not reveal specific arrhythmias. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no abnorzmalities. EEG was remarkable for dysrrhythmic waves and low amplitude voltage compatible with hypoxic encephalopathy. Although the definite cause of VF was not determined, it was recommended that the patient takes a beta-blocker (atenolol, 12.5 mg bid). She then underwent rehabilitation for cognitive function defects which resulted from hypoxic brain damage. She did not suffer any more attacks and stopped taking atenolol after several years.
Upon this ER arrival, the patient was unconscious, pulseless, and without spontaneous respirations. Blood pressure was undetectable, and her body temperature was 36.5℃. The initial ECG showed VF. Normal sinus rhythm was restored after 2 monophasic direct current defibrillations at 200 J (). On chest X-ray, no cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion was observed. The laboratory test results were as follows: white blood cell count, 12,400/mm3; hemoglobin, 14.5 g/dL; platelet count, 188,000/mm3; sodium, 138 mmol/L; potassium, 5.7 mmol/L; chloride, 111 mmol/L; ionized calcium, 1.42 mmol/L; ionized magnesium, 1.06 mmol/L; creatine kinase, 124 U/L; and creatine kinase-MB, 0.9 ng/mL. An arterial blood gas test revealed the following: pH 7.13; PaCO2, 55.5 mmHg; PaO2, 59.8 mmHg; HCO3, 17.7 mmol/L; and SaO2, 80.1%.
After defibrillation and intubation, the patient was moved to the coronary care unit (CCU). During nasogastric tube insertion, VF redeveloped. Sinus rhythm was successfully restored by 2 defibrillations at 200 J. A review of telemetry monitoring in the CCU revealed that sinus tachycardia precipitated bidirectional ventricular tachycardia that in turn degenerated into VF ().
The patient was diagnosed with CPVT accompanied by typical bidirectional ventricular tachycardia which was triggered by sinus tachycardia. After intravenously administered beta-blocker (labetalol, 10 mg), tachyarrhythmia was no longer observed. After stabilization, echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 68% without any structural abnormalities. She was prescribed an oral beta-blocker (metoprolol, 100 mg bid) and discharged from hospital. She is currently being followed up.

A 70-year-old Nigerian man presented at the emergency unit of our hospital with a 2 weeks history of abdominal pain. The pain was epigastric; severe, deep-seated, progressive, non-radiating, not relieved by food intake and not associated with vomiting or diarrhea. His condition worsened 5 days to presentation with generalized abdominal pain and abdominal wall rigidity. There was no change in bowel habit, no blood in stool, no abdominal distension, no associated fever, weight loss, alcohol binge or trauma. No history of previous medication, PUD or abdominal surgery, not a known diabetic, hypertensive, epileptic, asthmatic or sickler but has a history of moderate alcohol and cigarette use of more than 20 years. On clinical examination was an elderly man, conscious and alert but in obvious painful distress. He was afebrile, not pale, anicteric, not cyanosed, no pedal edema but was moderately dehydrated. The respiratory rate was 60 breaths per minute, pulse rate – 120 beats per minute and blood pressure 100/70 mmHg. The abdomen was flat, tense, and with minimal movement on respiration, marked generalized abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness, and rigidity. The examination of the liver, spleen, kidneys, and rectum were unremarkable but the prostate was moderately enlarged. An impression of peritonitis 2° to perforated PUD was made and he was placed on omeprazole, tramadol, paracetamol, flagyl, ceftriaxone, hydrocortisone, and fluid hydration. The preoperative laboratory investigations were hemoglobin concentration - 13 g/dl, serum electrolyte concentration - sodium (Na+) - 138 mmol/L, potassium (K+) - 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate (HCO3−) - 20 mmol/L, chloride (Cl−) - 108 mmol/L, and negative HIV 1 and 2 antibodies. Abdominal ultrasonography showed intraperitoneal echo-rich collection with dilated small bowel loops. The patient measured 1.67 m tall, weighed 60 kg, and had a body mass index of 21.5 kg/m2. An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed and a 3.1 cm by 1 cm gastric perforation covered with fibrinous exudate was seen with vegetative material within the peritoneum. An edge biopsy of the ulcerated perforation was taken and an omental patch repair and peritoneal lavage with normal saline was done. The gross examination of the specimen showed pieces of irregular grayish white tissues aggregating to 0.7 cm × 0.4 cm × 0.2 cm. The microscopic examination of the specimen showed an intense Candida growth consisting of numerous spores and budding hyphae [Figures and ] invading and destroying the gastric wall with marked granulation tissue formation, intense mixed inflammatory cell infiltration consisting of mainly eosinophils, macrophages, plasma cells, and lymphocytes. No Helicobacter pylori like organisms or atypical cellular proliferations were seen. A histopathological diagnosis of gastric perforation from invasive candidiasis was made and the patient was subsequently treated with fluconazole, clindamycin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, imipenem, tamsulosin, and discharged home after an uneventful postoperative period.

The patient specifically denied fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, or headache. His prescribed medications included atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia, Diltiazem and Lisinopril for hypertension, Metformin for diabetes, and Gabapentin for diabetic neuropathy. The patient had no allergies and his tetanus status was up to date.
Patient's vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 145/85 mmHg; respiratory rate 20/min; pulse 91/min, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C; and pain 8/10. The metabolic panel revealed blood sugar of 398 and corresponding hyponatremia of 128 mmol/L. AP and lateral radiographs of the left femur revealed mottled lucencies consistent with gas in the soft tissues of the medial thigh ().
A duplex Doppler exam with real time grey-scale imaging, spectral Doppler with wave form analysis, color Doppler, and physiologic maneuvers including compression were done to evaluate the venous system of the left leg from the groin down through the popliteal fossa. It is unclear exactly as to when the valproic acid sprinkles was started, but it appears that the patient was taking this drug for at least the last month prior to her hospitalization.
On admission examination, the patient was noted to be perseveratively calling out and crying. Her vital signs were stable, and she was uncooperative to the examination. She was underweight, at 66 inches in height, 99 lbs in weight, and body mass index (BMI) = 16 kg/m2. Despite her history of hypertension, her blood pressure (BP) on admission was low at 96/57 mm hg. She was noted to have a dysconjugate gaze. She had marked jerking movements of her upper extremities consistent with myoclonus. Muscle tone was increased, and it was difficult to assess for cogwheeling, as patient was unable to voluntarily relax her extremities. Myoclonus in her lower extremities was also noted when her feet were dorsiflexed. She was disoriented to time, place, and person and was unable to participate in a formal cognitive testing.
Laboratory examination on admission revealed a low serum albumin of 3.4 gm/dL. Her ammonia level was low normal at 4 umol/L. Complete blood count (CBC) was normal with a white cell count of 8100/cmm, a hemoglobin level of 13.7 gm/dL, and a hematocrit of 41.2%.

The patient was a 39-year-old woman who was referred to the renal division because of repeated glucosuria. She had no polyuria, polydipsia, or weight loss. Her blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, and her body weight was 55 kg. Routine urinary analysis showed 2+ to 3+ glucose with no other abnormalities. A quantitative test for urine glucose was 7.56 g/24 h. Her medical history and clinical examination revealed no significant findings. Fasting plasma glucose (4.92 mmol/l), albumin (42.8 g/l), creatinine (97 μmol/l), sodium (139.80 mmol/l), chloride (138.5 mmol/l), potassium (3.92 mmol/l), calcium (2.10 mmol/l), phosphate (1.04 mmol/l), magnesium (1.08 mmol/l), bicarbonate (19.4 mmol/l), uric acid (79 μmol/l), and hemoglobin A1C (5.3 %) were all within normal ranges. One hundred healthy Chinese volunteers (200 chromosomes) were included as controls. Informed written consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation in the study.
Genomic DNA was extracted by salting out from peripheral white blood cells. The entire coding region and adjacent intronic segments of SLC5A2 were screened for mutations by the direct sequencing of PCR products. The genomic DNA reference sequences of SLC5A2 (NG_012892.1, Gene ID: 6524, MIM: 182381, GEO Profiles ID: 62739973 and 65974292) and protein reference sequences of SGLT2 (NP_003032, UniProtKB - P31639) were acquired from the Entrez gene and protein database, respectively. To exclude the possibility that the identified mutations represented common polymorphisms, control chromosomes were tested by PCR-restriction-fragment length polymorphism. A novel missense SLC5A2 mutation was found in the patient (c.1891G > A/p.E631K, Fig. ). The amino acid residue (631E) was found to be highly conserved among human SGLT subtypes and across SGLT2 homologs in multiple species. The mutation was not detected in any of the control 200 chromosomes, indicating that it does not represent a common polymorphism.
Human SGLT2 cDNA from normal kidney, generated by reverse transcription (RT)-PCR, was cloned into the pGEM-T easy vector (Promega, Madison, WI). Wild-type and c.1891A mutagenized SLC5A2 generated by site-directed mutagenesis were subcloned into the PEXL-GFP vector [], and verified by sequencing. Human HEK293 cells (obtained from central laboratories of Peking Union Medical College Hospital, and originally from the American Type Culture Collection) were seeded into 24-well plates 24 h before transfection. Plasmid constructs (0.5 μg) were transfected into cultured cells at 70–80 % confluency using X-tremeGENE HP DNA transfection reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Roche, Mannheim, Germany). After 24 h of incubation, expression of SGLT2 wild type–GFP and mutant–GFP fusion proteins was detected by western blotting, confocal laser microscopy, and transport assays as we have done in previous studies [, ].
Western blotting analysis (Fig. ) demonstrated that 631 K SGLT2 expression was significantly lower than that of wild-type SGLT2–GFP (0.24 ± 0.14 vs. 1, P = 0.002, n = 4, Fig. ). Confocal imaging revealed that both the wild-type and mutant fusion proteins were expressed in a punctate pattern in the cell membrane, which merged well with the cell membrane marker 1,10-dioctadecyl-3,3,3’,3’-tetramethyl-indocarbocyanine perchlorate (DiIC18(3), Fig. ).
The function of wild-type SGLT2–GFP and 631 K SGLT2–GFP fusion proteins in cultured HEK293 cells was confirmed by transport of the glucose analog 2-(N-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3- diazol-4-yl)amino)-2-deoxyglucose (2-NBDG), evaluated by fluorescence intensity using flow cytometry. 2-NBDG uptake in HEK293 cells transfected with wild-type SGLT2–GFP was increased about 3.5-fold compared with those transfected with GFP-only control vector (7926 ± 1153 vs. 2314 ± 791, P < 0.001, n = 4, Fig. ). The uptake activity of the mutant SGLT2 631 K-GFP fusion protein was significantly decreased compared with wild-type SGLT2–GFP (3629 ± 1082 vs. 7926 ± 1153, P < 0.001, n = 4, Fig. ).
The Medical Ethics Committee of the Inner Mongolia People’s Hospital and Peking University approved the protocol. Data were compared with the t-test or analysis of variance followed by Fisher’s least significant difference methods for multiple comparisons. Data are shown as the mean ± SD, and significant differences were declared at P < 0.05.
Kidney proximal tubules reabsorb almost 180 g glucose daily, which is filtered through the glomeruli. SGLT2 accounts for most glucose reabsorption. It is responsible for the active transport of glucose across the brush border membrane, and is expressed almost exclusively in the kidney []. Recent studies have reported that SLC5A2 mutations are causative of FRG [, , –]. The long-term outcome of FRG patients is excellent, so SGLT2 inhibitors have been the subject of particular attention for the treatment of diabetes [, ]. Although research into FRG may help with a breakthrough for diabetes treatment, expression and functional studies of SLC5A2 mutations in FRG are rare, and the role of SGLT2 C-terminal mutations needs further clarification.
A previous study [] suggested that overt glucosuria requires the individual to be homozygous or compound heterozygous for SLC5A2 mutations. Consistent with this, our patient with a heterozygous mutation had “mild” glucosuria (urine glucose excretion, 7.56 g/day). However, our findings still imply that the mutation causes a clinically relevant SGLT2 dysfunction. Our in vitro study of 293 cells showed that the transport activity of the mutant SGLT2 631 K-GFP fusion proteins was significantly lower than that of wild-type. SLC5A2 mutations may reduce or abolish transporter activity by impairing protein synthesis, processing, or insertion into the plasma membrane. Furthermore, transporter activity may be reduced or abolished by accelerating protein removal or degradation, altering functional regulation, or impairing intrinsic activity. The mutant SGLT2 631 K–GFP in our study had a similar punctate membrane expression pattern to wild-type, but a decreased expression intensity. Thus, the mutation (c.1891G > A/p.E631K) is likely to impair protein synthesis or accelerate protein removal or degradation. Our results also suggest that the SGLT2 C-terminal is very important for protein expression levels. We speculate that the reduced expression of the SGLT2 mutant is responsible for the decreased transport activity of mutant SGLT2.
Although it was not possible to perform a family study in the present case, identification of mutations that cause glucosuria will enable the establishment of a genotypic FRG diagnosis, providing important information for families and physicians. In general, renal biopsies are unnecessary for FRG patients, so the effect of the 631 K mutation on SGLT2 expression in the kidney is still unknown. We were restricted to an in vitro study of the expression and function of SGLT2 using GFP as a fluorescent label because we previously found that the SGLT2 antibody was unsuited to use in 293 cells, COS-7 cells, and Xenopus laevis oocytes.

An 82-year-old male who resides in a skilled nursing facility was brought to the emergency department this morning after several days of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with rust-colored sputum, and subjective fevers noted by the facility staff on their overnight rounds. According to the transfer notes, he was last seen in his usual state of health four days earlier; since then he has refused two therapy sessions because of fatigue but has remained lucid, conversing normally with nurses and easily redirectable, without any reports of confusion or disorientation. Past medical history is significant for long-standing hypertension and stage 3b chronic kidney disease attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis; his most recent outpatient serum creatinine two months ago was 2.1 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate in the mid-20s. He has no known history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, cirrhosis, or cancer, and he has never been diagnosed with congestive heart failure. He does not smoke and has not consumed alcohol for decades; all medications, including an ACE inhibitor, calcium-channel blocker, and low-dose aspirin, were taken as prescribed up until yesterday when oral intake began to wane because of malaise. Upon arrival he is seated upright on the stretcher, breathing rapidly but able to complete short sentences; he remains alert, answers questions appropriately, and names the month and location without difficulty. Initial vital signs prior to any interventions reveal an oral temperature of 39.1 °C, pulse 88 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, blood pressure 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation in the low 80s on room air, improving modestly with application of 2 L/min nasal cannula. Physical examination demonstrates flushed, warm skin; dry mucous membranes; and faint inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung field with dullness to percussion posteriorly. No jugular venous distention or peripheral edema is appreciated. Cardiac auscultation discloses a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs. Abdominal examination is benign, and there are no focal neurologic deficits. Point-of-care capillary glucose is 140 mg/dL. Laboratory studies drawn immediately, before the patient received fluids or antipyretics, show a hematocrit of 42 %, serum sodium 138 mEq/L, and blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL; creatinine is modestly above baseline at 2.3 mg/dL. Venous lactate is mildly elevated at 2.1 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas obtained on 2 L nasal cannula reveals pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, PaO₂ 55 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L. Portable chest radiograph, reviewed at the bedside, demonstrates a consolidation in the right lower lobe with blunting of the right costophrenic angle suggestive of an accompanying small pleural effusion; no parenchymal abnormalities are seen on the contralateral side. Electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. Urinalysis is bland aside from trace protein, consistent with his known kidney impairment. The nursing home director reports that influenza vaccination was administered this season, but pneumococcal vaccination status is uncertain. The patient denies recent hospitalization, exposure to sick contacts, or aspiration events. At this time he has not yet received antibiotics, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics; blood cultures, sputum culture, and nasopharyngeal swabs have been sent, and he is pending further diagnostic imaging to quantify the pleural fluid collection. The initial impression is community-acquired pneumonia involving the right lower lobe with an associated small effusion in an elderly gentleman with underlying chronic renal insufficiency and mild hypoxemia.

He had never been diagnosed with any malignancy and had no history of liver inflammation, alcohol-related disease, or viral hepatitis. The patient lives with his spouse in their own single-level home and remains fully independent in dressing, bathing, cooking, and driving; he explicitly denied any recent stays in skilled-nursing facilities, rehabilitation centers, or congregate living environments. Two weeks before presentation he completed his seasonal influenza vaccination and had not taken antibiotics during the current illness. On arrival he was seated upright on the examination table, conversing coherently and oriented to date, location, and situation without confusion, lethargy, or agitation. Her hip pain has progressed over the past year to the point that, during the last week, she has required assistance for nearly every transfer from bed to chair and spends most of the day recumbent with pillows supporting the limb, venturing out of the room only for brief, guarded trips to the bathroom with a front-wheel walker. She states that aside from these short excursions, she has effectively remained in bed for the past four consecutive days. Of note, she is still within the first month of recovery from an open abdominal hysterectomy performed 27 days ago for symptomatic leiomyomata that failed medical management; that operation was uncomplicated, the midline incision now shows healthy granulation, and she has not experienced fever, wound drainage, or systemic infection since discharge. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exertional chest pressure, palpitations, or lower-limb tightness suggesting fluid overload, and an echocardiogram obtained last year for evaluation of palpitations showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction with normal valves. Respiratory history is unremarkable; she never smoked, uses no inhalers, and relates no episodes of wheeze, chronic cough, or oxygen dependence. Twenty years ago she was diagnosed with left-sided ulcerative colitis after colonoscopy with biopsy; flares have been infrequent and are well controlled on oral mesalamine 2.4 g daily, with her last course of prednisone more than five years ago. She has never required colectomy and denies current abdominal pain, tenesmus, or rectal bleeding. She explicitly recalls no episode of clots in the legs or lungs and has never undergone duplex ultrasonography or CT pulmonary angiography; her parents, siblings, and adult children are likewise free of unexplained venous events. She was exposed to unfractionated heparin during a prior cholecystectomy without any fall in platelet count, and outside records reveal normal coagulation studies and absence of antiphospholipid antibodies when these were checked by her gastroenterologist several years ago because of IBD. Symptoms resolved completely within two weeks after inpatient rehabilitation, and she was discharged on aspirin 81 mg daily and high-intensity rosuvastatin, which she has taken reliably; she has had no subsequent focal neurologic complaints, gait disturbance, or visual episodes, and annual neurologic reviews remain stable. She arrived unaccompanied by taxi, declined the elevator, and climbed one flight of stairs to reception at a measured pace without needing to pause. At home she prepares meals, gardens in raised beds for thirty minutes at a time, and can slowly ascend two residential flights while carrying a laundry basket, all without chest tightness, palpitations, or unexpected dyspnea. She sleeps flat, has not awakened gasping, and has noted no ankle swelling or sudden weight gain. Strength and language returned over subsequent weeks, and she completed outpatient speech and physical therapy; neurologic follow-up last month documented normal gait, intact cranial nerves, and only subtle word-finding difficulty when fatigued. Since that cerebrovascular event she has taken clopidogrel 75 mg daily in addition to atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and follows a low-sodium, heart-healthy diet recommended by her primary physician. Her other chronic conditions include well-controlled hypertension managed with amlodipine 5 mg each morning and lisinopril 10 mg at bedtime, stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to long-standing renovascular hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed eight years earlier after fasting glucose values in the 140s; lifestyle modification plus metformin extended release 1000 mg twice daily have kept her most recent hemoglobin A1c at 7.0 %, and she has never used injectable glucose-lowering therapy. She has never experienced exertional angina, has not undergone coronary angiography, stress imaging, or revascularization, and serial electrocardiograms remain free of pathologic Q waves or ischemic ST-T changes. Respiratory history is limited to mild seasonal allergic rhinitis; she has never smoked, quit social cigar use in her twenties, drinks one glass of red wine on holidays, and denies recreational drug exposure. Past operations include uncomplicated bilateral cataract extractions five years ago. Family history reveals a brother who required carotid endarterectomy at 69 and a mother who succumbed to ruptured intracranial aneurysm at 80; there is no family record of premature coronary death. Jugular venous pulse is not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth interspace, mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation discloses a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2 without gallop or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout with good diaphragmatic excursion. Abdominal examination demonstrates a palpable, expansile, non-tender mid-line mass just above the umbilicus consistent with the known aneurysm; there is no guard, rebound, or flank tenderness. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric in femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial distributions; no peripheral edema or skin discoloration is present. Neurologic screening reveals full orientation, fluent speech with occasional word searching, 5/5 strength in all extremities, symmetric reflexes, intact sensation, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before the visit show hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, white blood cell count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.51 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 44 mL/min/1.73 m². Here is a patient note:
A 63-year-old woman with no prior history of chronic lung disease, heart failure, chronic kidney or liver dysfunction, malignancy, or use of immunosuppressive medications was transported to the medical intensive care unit directly from the emergency department after being discovered at home with progressive dyspnea and fever that had worsened over the preceding twenty-four hours. According to family, she had complained the previous evening of pleuritic chest discomfort and a dry cough that began two days earlier, but she declined to seek care until the morning of admission, when she became increasingly confused and was noted to breathe rapidly even at rest. Emergency medical services found her sitting upright, flushed, and tachypneic; oxygen saturation was 74 % on ambient air, so the crew placed a tight-fitting face mask connected to a blender delivering approximately 70 % inspired oxygen during the short transport. No intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, corticosteroids, or vasoactive agents were started in the field or in the emergency bay prior to transfer. On arrival to the ICU—still breathing the same high-concentration oxygen and before any therapeutic intervention—her vital signs were: oral temperature 101.8 °F, heart rate 109 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute with moderate accessory muscle use, and noninvasive blood pressure 108/63 mm Hg confirmed by a second cuff reading. She opened her eyes only when addressed loudly, spoke in disoriented sentences, and followed motor commands in all extremities, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 12 without sedatives or paralytics on board. Skin examination showed warm, moist integument without cyanosis or mottling; capillary refill was brisk. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated, cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs or gallops, distal pulses were equal, and there was no peripheral edema. Lung fields were diffusely dull to percussion with coarse inspiratory crackles most pronounced over the right middle and lower zones, and breath sounds were markedly diminished at both bases. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds; flank percussion produced no costovertebral tenderness. Extremities were warm with full passive range of motion, and there were no focal neurologic deficits. A radial arterial blood sample obtained within ten minutes of unit arrival, while she remained on 70 % FiO₂, demonstrated a pH of 7.30, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, PaO₂ 62 mm Hg, and a calculated alveolar-arterial gradient of 427 mm Hg, indicating severe impairment of oxygen transfer. Routine laboratory studies drawn simultaneously revealed serum sodium 148 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 107 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.45 mg/dL, the latter slightly higher than her last documented outpatient value of 1.1 mg/dL eight months earlier but without oliguria or hematuria noted—in the emergency department she had produced 200 mL of clear yellow urine through a freshly placed Foley catheter. The complete blood count showed a white cell count of 15 500 /mm³ with 86 % neutrophils and moderate left shift, hematocrit 31 %, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and platelets 196 000 /mm³. Coagulation parameters were within reference limits, and serum lactate measured 2.1 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before antibiotics demonstrated bilateral patchy airspace opacities with right lower-lobe predominance and no overt pleural effusion or cardiomegaly. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound revealed a small, collapsible inferior vena cava and preserved left ventricular systolic function, arguing against cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Electrocardiography performed on admission showed normal sinus rhythm at 108 beats per minute without ischemic changes. She denied tobacco use for more than a decade, drinks wine only on holidays, and reported no recent travel, aspiration events, or sick contacts. Vaccinations are reportedly up to date except for missing the most recent influenza booster. Blood cultures, sputum for Gram stain and culture, and a rapid respiratory viral panel were collected immediately after the arterial puncture, but no antimicrobial, fluid bolus, or vasopressor had been administered at the moment the physiologic data above were documented.

A 65-year-old man, previously independent and working part-time as a school bus driver, was transferred from the emergency department to the surgical intensive care unit for physiologic monitoring after presenting with twenty-four hours of colicky periumbilical pain, progressive abdominal distention, and more than a dozen episodes of greenish, non-bloody emesis that began shortly after he ate leftover casserole the night before admission. He has a history of well-controlled essential hypertension managed with low-dose lisinopril, remote open appendectomy in his early twenties, and no diabetes, chronic lung disease, chronic liver disease, malignancy, organ transplantation, or use of corticosteroids, cytotoxic drugs, or biologic agents. According to his spouse he takes no over-the-counter supplements, drinks alcohol only at family gatherings, has never smoked, and has not been hospitalized in the last decade. Paramedics found him seated upright on the sofa, retching into a bucket yet conversant and oriented, with an oxygen saturation in the upper 80s on ambient air; they applied a Venturi mask delivering 45 % inspired oxygen but administered no intravenous fluids, antiemetics, analgesics, or antibiotics during the brief ten-minute transport. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—and before any emergency department interventions—vital signs were documented as oral temperature 99.2 °F (37.3 °C), heart rate 101 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 33 breaths per minute with shallow subcostal movement, and automated blood pressure 120/67 mm Hg confirmed manually. He was seated, leaning forward, clutching his abdomen, but opened his eyes spontaneously, carried on a coherent conversation about the events leading up to admission, and obeyed multi-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 without sedatives, opioids, or intoxicants on board. Skin examination revealed dry oral mucosa and reduced axillary moisture; capillary refill was brisk and no peripheral cyanosis, jaundice, or petechiae were present. Neck veins were flat at 30°, heart sounds were crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, peripheral pulses were easily palpable, and no peripheral edema was noted. Lungs were clear to auscultation except for faint bibasilar crackles likely related to atelectasis from abdominal splinting; there were no wheezes or rhonchi. The distended abdomen exhibited visible peristaltic waves, high-pitched “tinkling” bowel sounds, and diffuse tympany on percussion; palpation elicited guarding but no rebound, and there was no flank ecchymosis or inguinal hernia. Digital rectal examination yielded scant brown stool without blood. Extremities were warm and neurologically intact, and he ambulates with a steady gait when encouraged to stand. A radial arterial blood gas drawn ten minutes after triage while he remained on the same 45 % FiO₂ mask revealed pH 7.39, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 64 mm Hg, consistent with normocapnia and mild hypoxemia uncorrected by moderate supplemental oxygen, most likely secondary to basal collapse from diaphragmatic elevation. Simultaneous laboratory studies obtained from the same arterial stick showed serum sodium 151 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, chloride 114 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.25 mg/dL—slightly higher than his documented baseline of 1.0 mg/dL one year earlier but without oliguria, hematuria, or casts on urinalysis, suggesting prerenal concentration from vomiting-induced volume depletion rather than intrinsic kidney injury. Point-of-care glucose measured 122 mg/dL, calcium 9.2 mg/dL, and lactate 1.7 mmol/L. Complete blood count demonstrated white blood cell count 13 800 /mm³ with 80 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, and platelets 243 000 /µL; peripheral smear showed no blasts, schistocytes, or toxic granulation. Portable supine abdominal radiograph obtained before any nasogastric decompression displayed markedly dilated central small-bowel loops with several air-fluid levels and a relative paucity of colonic gas, without free intraperitoneal air. A limited, upright chest film performed concurrently showed elevated hemidiaphragms and bibasilar plate-like atelectasis but no focal consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma was negative for free fluid; bedside ultrasound of the inferior vena cava revealed >50 % collapsibility with inspiration, supporting intravascular depletion. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound demonstrated a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle and no pericardial effusion. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm at 100 beats per minute, normal PR and QT intervals, and nonspecific ST-T wave changes without acute ischemia. A nasogastric tube was not yet inserted, no intravenous crystalloids had been started, and no antiemetic, opioid, proton-pump inhibitor, or broad-spectrum antibiotic had been given at the moment the decision was made to transfer him to the ICU for aggressive fluid resuscitation, serial electrolyte monitoring focused on the hypernatremia, early decompression of the obstructed small bowel, and readiness for operative intervention should evidence of strangulation or perforation develop; consequently, all physiologic measurements and laboratory values above reflect his untreated baseline state at the time of unit acceptance.

A previously healthy 43-year-old woman was transferred directly from the emergency department to the medical intensive care unit after developing abrupt, crushing dyspnea and light-headedness while climbing a single flight of stairs in her apartment building three hours earlier. She had returned from a trans-Pacific business trip the night before, spending more than twelve hours seated, and complained to her roommate of a mild cramp in the right calf that morning but otherwise felt well enough to go grocery shopping. Her background is notable only for a combined estrogen–progestin oral contraceptive taken for menorrhagia; she has never required long-term steroids, dialysis, chemotherapy, or any organ transplant, has no history of chronic lung, kidney, or liver disease, and denies autoimmune or hematologic disorders. She smokes fewer than five cigarettes per week, drinks wine socially, and uses no recreational drugs. Family history is free of premature venous thromboembolism. Emergency medical services arrived within ten minutes of the call to find her sitting upright, gasping, and clutching the anterior chest but still speaking in short phrases. Peripheral pulse oximetry on ambient air registered in the low 70-percent range, prompting placement of a Venturi mask later measured in triage to deliver 42 % inspired oxygen; no intravenous fluids, anticoagulants, analgesics, or vasopressors were administered en route. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital-initiated therapy—her temperature by temporal scanner was 98.9 °F, radial pulse 88 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute with visibly increased work, and noninvasive blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg confirmed by repeat manual cuff. Skin was warm and well perfused, capillary refill was under two seconds, and there was no cyanosis or mottling. Jugular venous pulsations were not elevated at 30 degrees. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and single S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses were symmetric and of normal amplitude. Pulmonary examination demonstrated clear breath sounds over the apices but markedly diminished air entry at both bases with faint, dry crackles and no wheeze; percussion was resonant throughout. Abdomen was soft and nontender with active bowel sounds, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic screening showed equal and reactive pupils, intact cranial nerves, and brisk deep-tendon reflexes. Inspection of the extremities identified subtle circumferential fullness of the right calf compared with the left yet no erythema, warmth, or palpable cord; Homans sign was not elicited. A radial arterial sample drawn within ten minutes of stretcher placement, while she remained on the 42 % oxygen source, disclosed a pH of 7.52, partial pressure of oxygen 55 mm Hg, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg, indicating marked respiratory alkalosis with significant hypoxemia relative to the delivered fraction of inspired oxygen. Simultaneously drawn laboratory studies revealed serum sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, chloride 105 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, glucose 108 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 9 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL; urine output since emergency department arrival totaled 120 mL of clear yellow fluid over ninety minutes. Complete blood count showed a white-cell count of 9 700 /mm³ with 72 % neutrophils, hematocrit 43 %, hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, and platelets 255 000/µL. Cardiac troponin was pending at the moment of transfer, and D-dimer returned elevated at 3.2 µg/mL FEU. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound performed before any anticoagulation demonstrated a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with preserved left-sided systolic function, a flattened interventricular septum, and a small, collapsible inferior vena cava; lung ultrasound revealed patchy subpleural consolidations without pleural effusion. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained prior to radiologic contrast showed clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, and no parenchymal infiltrate or effusion.
